edbDesc: (sometimes known as streamline flow) Occurs when a fluid flows in parallel layers, with no disruption between the layers. In fluid dynamics, laminar flow is a flow regime characterized by high momentum diffusion, low momentum convection, pressure and velocity independent from time. It is the opposite of turbulent flow. In nonscientific terms laminar flow is 'smooth,' while turbulent flow is 'rough.'
title: Laminar flow
description: Slow or narrow flows slide along in smooth, parallel layers; speed them up and they break into churning eddies. Osborne Reynolds showed in 1883, with a thread of dye in a glass pipe, that a single number predicts which you get. Smooth flow means far less drag and clean, predictable streams.
effect: slow or narrow flows move in smooth layers instead of churning
strength: Water in a 1 cm pipe stays smooth below about 20 cm/s; keeping air laminar over a wing cuts skin drag there several-fold.
pickWhy: Borderline: Judgment call: a flow regime rather than an effect, and it could share one Reynolds card with Turbulence (another batch); picked keep since smooth flow itself does a job.
